performers: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London; Artur Rodzinski, conductor
question: What do the ending’s repeated notes and sustained weight make you hear—and which conclusions belong to interpretation rather than documented fact?
intro: The finale moves from a forceful march through a much quieter middle to a repeated-note ending in D major. Rodzinski’s Westminster performance is reported to contain a 37-bar cut; this package presents the supplied track intact, not an uncut realization of the score.

sections.label: Opening march
sections.mNote: Brass and timpani establish the forceful opening.

sections.label: Quiet middle · approximate
sections.mNote: The large opening wave gives way to reduced sound.

sections.label: Rebuilding passage
sections.mNote: Activity resumes gradually; cut location remains unaligned.

sections.label: Orchestral return · approximate
sections.mNote: March character regains weight in the later build.

sections.label: Final repeated-note field
sections.mNote: Late coda region, not the exact D-major arrival.

cues.title: Brass before strings
cues.text: A powerful opening attack introduces the brass-led march with timpani. The strings initially rest. Listen to the directness of that instrumental choice after the Largo, where the brass family was absent throughout.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed p. 109, rehearsal 97: opening wind/brass sonority and timpani, strings resting; brass march follows. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: first strong five-second window at 0:05 reaches −4.7 dB. This concerns the opening passage, not the exact first attack sample.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The march finds moving layers
cues.text: The opening does not remain one block of brass. Winds and strings add more mobile figures around the march’s strongly marked profile. Follow the moving surface separately from the heavier punctuation underneath it.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed p. 111 and following, rehearsal 98: winds and strings become active after the brass-led opening. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: the first minute alternates stronger and lighter windows rather than sustaining the opening peak. Regional placement only.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cut in this performance
cues.text: A discographic review of Rodzinski’s Westminster recordings reports the same 37-bar finale cut found in his earlier account. That matters here: this is the complete supplied track, but not an uncut finale. The cut’s exact position has not been established in this transfer.
cues.evidence: https://www.opusklassiek.nl/cd-recensies/cd-nn/nnrodzinski_westminster.htm, Niek Nelissen, August 2026: the 1942 account is described as omitting 37 bars; the Westminster discussion explicitly says Rodzinski made the same cut. This is a source-attributed version claim, not an audio splice located at 1:20. No alternate recording is used.

cues.title: Forward motion with changing weight
cues.text: The march’s force is not a constant loud plateau. Notice the changes of weight within the span: the rhythm can continue to project forward even as the orchestral sound becomes less or more dense.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: 1:35–2:30 windows vary from approximately −16 to −11 dB, following a stronger −7.0 window at 1:30. This cue describes measured dynamic contour, not a metronome or formal-bar alignment.

cues.title: The first great wave
cues.text: The opening span gathers into its largest measured crest before the quiet middle. Hear the increasing weight across the whole wave, not just the final loud instant; the subsequent withdrawal depends on that accumulated scale.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: level rises from −11.1 dB at 2:30 to −7.1 at 2:35 and reaches the movement’s loudest five-second window, −4.0, at 3:05.

cues.title: An enormous change of scale
cues.text: The strong opening region gives way to an exceptionally quiet middle. Keep the reduced sound in focus rather than mentally carrying the previous volume forward: the same transfer now asks for a very different scale of listening.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: boundaries at 3:16 and 3:20; level falls from −7.1 dB at 3:10 to −18.0 at 3:15 and −31.8 at 3:20. The precise score bar and any relation to the reported cut are not established.

cues.title: An optimism stated in print
cues.text: A 1956 introduction published under Shostakovich’s name described the finale as an optimistic resolution of the symphony’s conflicts. That is a documented public account. It does not by itself settle his private intentions or require every listener to experience the ending as uncomplicated triumph.
cues.evidence: https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en, quotation from the introduction to the 1956 score, describing the individual’s formation and the finale’s optimistic outlet. The cue distinguishes a published statement from an authenticated private explanation.

cues.title: The middle grows quieter still
cues.text: The quiet middle does not simply hold one level. It recedes further, making the eventual return a long recovery of weight rather than an immediate restart of the opening.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: levels fall from approximately −20 to −25 dB around 4:10–4:25 to −29.9 at 4:50 and −34.1 at 5:05. No programme or exact cut location is inferred from this contour.

cues.title: Testimony is a contested source
cues.text: The often-repeated “forced rejoicing” reading is associated with Testimony, published by Solomon Volkov in 1979 as Shostakovich’s memoirs. The book’s authenticity is disputed. That interpretation can be discussed, but it is not presented here as an established explanation of the finale.
cues.evidence: Alex Ross reports the publication and Laurel Fay’s documentary challenge in Unauthorized, The New Yorker, 2004: https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2004/09/06/unauthorized . Additional controversy bibliography: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testimony_%28Volkov_book%29 . Ross’s own judgments are not adopted as a final verdict; the cue neither authenticates a private Shostakovich statement nor identifies a coded message at this timestamp.

cues.title: The return is built gradually
cues.text: The recovery of orchestral weight takes time. Listen for renewed activity before the sound becomes forceful again: rebuilding is part of the form, not merely a corridor between the quiet middle and the final tutti.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: strongest boundaries at 5:12 and 5:24 precede another quiet interval; levels then rise from −29.7 dB at 5:55 to −23.9 at 6:15 and −20.4 at 6:30. No exact rehearsal-number alignment is claimed.

cues.title: March weight returns
cues.text: The later build restores the march’s orchestral weight. Compare this return with the abrupt opening: here the force has to emerge from a long period of reduced sound, so its arrival has a different history in your ear.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, later finale buildup, printed pp. 146–158, including renewed percussion, winds, strings and brass. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: boundaries at 6:38 and 6:50; level rises to −8.8 dB at 6:50. The reported cut prevents a bar-proportional map from being treated as exact.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeated notes, sustained weight
cues.text: In the closing D-major region, repeated high notes continue above much longer brass and bass tones. Listen to the friction between those two time-scales. The key and the repeated-note texture are written facts; whether they sound celebratory, insistent or troubling is an interpretive judgment.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed pp. 158–165: D-major closing region, repeated A figures and sustained brass/bass writing. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: late boundaries at 7:06 and 7:16 precede the final sustained level region. The cue is not the exact point of modulation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An emphatic written ending
cues.text: The score ends with heavily accented final chords and percussion, not a fade. Let that physical fact stand before choosing a narrative for it: an unequivocal ending need not imply an unequivocal meaning.
cues.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, printed p. 165: final sustained chords and percussion accents, including bass drum. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: level is −7.9 dB at 8:00 and falls to −21.6 at 8:05; decoded duration 489.6 seconds. The exact release is not sample-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The first wave releases its weight
transitions.how: The forceful first span withdraws into a dramatically reduced region. The change in level and texture is unmistakable in this transfer; its precise score location is not established, and it is not labelled as the position of the reported cut.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: −4.0 dB at 3:05 falls to −31.8 at 3:20; boundaries at 3:16 and 3:20. Score context: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, pp. 136–142. Cut documentation: https://www.opusklassiek.nl/cd-recensies/cd-nn/nnrodzinski_westminster.htm.

transitions.title: Activity resumes before full force returns
transitions.how: A marked change in the quiet region restarts the process of accumulation. The transfer does not jump immediately to the final full sound; another reduced interval separates this activity from the later rise. The marker is acoustic, not an asserted thematic-entry bar.
transitions.evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: strongest boundary at 5:12, another at 5:24; level rises from −34.1 at 5:05 to −18.4 at 5:20, then withdraws again. No cut location is assigned.

transitions.title: The rebuild recovers orchestral mass
transitions.how: The later march region gains force through accumulation rather than the opening’s immediate impact. Increasing level and denser orchestral support carry the join. The return is a broad listening region; the exact first returning bar remains unaligned.
transitions.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, pp. 146–158. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: boundaries at 6:38 and 6:50, with level rising from −25.4 at 6:20 to −8.8 at 6:50.

transitions.title: Motion settles into repeated-note insistence
transitions.how: The late coda sets fast repeated upper notes against longer brass and bass tones. The marker identifies that closing field, not the exact D-major arrival. Its instrumental and rhythmic facts are described without deciding whether the result signifies victory, coercion or something else.
transitions.evidence: https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf, pp. 158–165: repeated A figures above the D-major closing support. cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony: late boundaries at 7:06/7:16 and sustained final activity. Political meaning is not derived from the audio features.

source.title: Symphony No. 5 — Muzgiz M. 16313 Г, historical full score
source.locator: Printed pp. 109–165; PDF pp. 111–167. The reported 37-bar cut (https://www.opusklassiek.nl/cd-recensies/cd-nn/nnrodzinski_westminster.htm) is not located; selected broad snapshots must not be read as an uncut bar map. Viewed score is public domain in Taiwan, not cleared for EU/US republication; exact performing edition unknown. Timing evidence: cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-finale.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony.

timeline.note: Opening wind/brass attack followed by brass march with timpani, p. 109; strings initially rest. Successive opening events grouped, not one static chord.
Moving wind/string layers after the opening, p. 111 and following; approximate regional snapshot.
Reduced string region after the opening wave, p. 138; acoustic withdrawal near 3:16–3:20. Exact page-to-time correspondence remains uncertain because the cut is unaligned.
Selected rebuilding texture from p. 146/rehearsal 121, including side drum within percussion; approximate correspondence to the gradual late recovery, not an exact entrance.
Later orchestral accumulation, pp. 156–158; selected active groups, not an exhaustive chord inventory or an uncut timing map.
D-major closing field, pp. 164–165: upper repeated notes, long brass tones and bass support; approximate late-coda snapshot.
Final sustained chords and percussion accents, p. 165; the last repeated-note attack and final chords occur successively in this closing snapshot.

fields.value: Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956
fields.note: The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

composer.epithet: Fifteen symphonies and fifteen quartets turn marches, fugues and a four-note signature into arguments about public ceremony and individual memory.
facts: Petrograd Conservatory from 1919: piano with Leonid Nikolayev, composition with Maximilian Steinberg
Leningrad Conservatory from 1937; Moscow Conservatory from 1943; dismissed from both in 1948
DSCH = D–E♭–C–B, using German note names
Fifteen symphonies · fifteen string quartets · six concertos · operas, songs and film scores
composer.background:
Dmitri Shostakovich was born in St Petersburg in 1906, the son of an engineer and a pianist. His mother, Sofiya, gave him his first piano lessons; in 1919 he entered the Petrograd Conservatory, where Leonid Nikolayev taught him piano and Maximilian Steinberg composition. The director, Alexander Glazunov, supported the young musician through the shortages following revolution and civil war. His father’s death in 1922 worsened the family’s finances, and Shostakovich earned money accompanying silent films. He graduated in piano in 1923 and composition in 1925: the graduation score was his First Symphony, written before his nineteenth birthday.

Nikolai Malko conducted its première in Leningrad on 12 May 1926. The orchestra includes a piano, whose abrupt interventions contribute to the symphonic argument. Clarinet, bassoon and trumpet exchange short phrases; a waltz can become a march without a change of personnel. International performances followed. Shostakovich still considered a performing career and received an honourable mention at the first Warsaw Chopin Competition in 1927. Thereafter his public piano appearances increasingly centred on his own works, including the concertos, chamber music and songs.
